correctness.rationale: Conditional on \(M_k=m\), every binary relevance vector has probability \(p^m(1-p)^{k-m}\), hence the conditional law is exactly uniform and independent of \(p\). Independent enumeration for all \(k\le8\) verified the submitted closed conditional-mean formula exactly. The source paper's online variance formula has leading term \(5p^3(1-p)/k\). Independently expanding the linear Hoeffding projection gives coefficients \(c_{i,k}=p+(1-p)/i+p(H_k-H_i)\); their normalized squared sum tends to 5. Differentiating the centering baseline contributes the projection on the total count, and the squared residual coefficients tend to 1, yielding the stated adjusted variance and the \(4+1\) split. Standard triangular-array Lindeberg plus negligibility of the degenerate quadratic remainder gives the two CLTs.
correctness.risk: The asymptotic claims require fixed interior \(p\in(0,1)\); boundary/sparse regimes need separate scaling.

value.rationale: The result converts an existing random-ranking benchmark into an exact finite-sample, prevalence-free test and quantifies precisely how much asymptotic fluctuation is attributable to estimating/conditioning out prevalence. That addresses the source paper's explicit testing gap and supplies a practically interpretable variance decomposition.

final_claim: Under the i.i.d. Bernoulli-\(p\) random-ranking model for online \(AP@k\), conditioning on the observed total \(M_k=m\) makes the relevance pattern uniform over all \(\binom{k}{m}\) binary strings and therefore gives an exact nuisance-free randomization test for unusually early relevant items. The conditional mean is \[\eta_{k,m}=\frac{mH_k}{k^2}+\frac{m(m-1)(k-H_k)}{k^2(k-1)},\] and for fixed \(p\in(0,1)\) the known-prevalence CLT has asymptotic variance \(5p^3(1-p)\), whereas centering by the plug-in conditional baseline reduces it to \(p^3(1-p)\), giving an exact asymptotic variance split \(4+1\).
limitations: The CLTs are for fixed \(p\in(0,1)\), not sparse or boundary prevalence.
The exact conditional test is conditional on the observed total and targets order effects, not prevalence itself.
